story_type: rocket camera through liftoff fire to space, weather satellite
hook: This camera rode up the side of a rocket, straight through the fire.
narration: A camera on the side of this rocket rode straight up through the launch fire.
The Atlas V lifted off from Cape Canaveral on March first, 2022, carrying a NOAA weather satellite called GOES-T.
Ninety seconds in, it weighed half of what it did at launch, burning more than two thousand six hundred pounds of propellant every second.
Solid rocket boosters give extra push off the pad. Once their fuel is gone they are dead weight, so they get cut loose.
[short pause] Then the empty boosters let go and tumbled away over the Earth.
Just over two minutes up, the camera was looking down on the curve of the Earth.
outcome: GOES-T separated from its rocket and flew on to help forecasters track hurricanes, tornadoes and wildfires.

location_card.place: Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida

title: Rocket camera rides through the fire
description:
Cameras on a United Launch Alliance Atlas V 541 watched the launch fire, the solid rocket boosters falling away and the curve of the Earth as NOAA's GOES-T weather satellite launched from Cape Canaveral, Florida, on March 1, 2022.

facts.source_quote: GOES-T is scheduled to launch on March 1, 2022 at 4:38 p.m. EST from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station (CCSFS) on a United Launch Alliance (ULA) Atlas V 541 rocket.

facts.claim: At 90 seconds the rocket weighed half its launch weight

facts.claim: Burning more than 2,600 pounds of propellant per second

SOBs have burned out as expected and we see a good SOB jettison.

facts.claim: Outcome: GOES-T separated and continued on to help observe hurricanes, tornadoes, forest fires
facts.source_quote: satellite separated from the spacecraft and is continuing on its journey to help meteorologists observe and predict local weather events, including thunderstorms, tornadoes, fog, hurricanes, flash floods and other severe weather.

extra_sources.excerpt: Following completion of a third planned start and then cutoff of the United Launch Alliance Atlas V 541 Centaur main engine, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA) Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite-T (GOES-T) satellite separated from the spacecraft and is continuing on its journey to help meteorologists observe and predict local weather events, including thunderstorms, tornadoes, fog, hurricanes, flash floods and other severe weather. In addition, GOES observations have proven helpful in monitoring dust storms, volcanic eruptions, and forest fires.
